claims.text: EARS (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) was developed by Alistair Mavin and colleagues at Rolls-Royce while analyzing airworthiness regulations for a jet engine control system; first published at IEEE International Requirements Engineering Conference (RE'09) in 2009.
claims.notes: Origin firmly established; not vendor-promoted.

claims.text: EARS has been adopted by organizations including Airbus, Bosch, Dyson, Honeywell, Intel, NASA, Rolls-Royce, and Siemens, and is taught at universities in multiple countries.
claims.notes: Industry adoption breadth confirms maturity.

claims.text: Amazon Kiro IDE (2025) adopted EARS as its native requirements notation; spec-driven workflow operates in three phases (requirements.md with EARS criteria, design.md, tasks.md).
claims.notes: Direct precedent for spec-driven AI workflow using EARS — same shape as our pipeline.

claims.text: EARS provides five templates: Ubiquitous (no keyword), Event-driven (When), Unwanted/Error (If-then), State-driven (While), Optional Feature (Where).
claims.notes: Standard template structure; corroborated across multiple sources.

claims.text: EARS is best suited for discrete event-driven systems and less effective for purely functional/mathematical systems; teams require training to apply EARS effectively, especially when transitioning from unstructured requirements.
claims.notes: Documented limitations; relevant to our pipeline which is largely event-driven.

claims.text: EARS-formatted specifications reduce ambiguity that causes AI agents to make undesirable assumptions; constrained natural language can be parsed by both humans and LLMs, bridging product intent and machine-readable specifications.
claims.notes: Direct evidence that EARS pays dividends in AI workflows specifically.

claims.text: Multi-agent failure analysis (MAST) found 36.9% of failures caused by inter-agent misalignment: conflicting outputs, context loss during handoffs, and incompatible conclusions reached independently — the consistency gap is one of the most underappreciated failure modes in parallel agentic systems.
claims.notes: Cross-corroborated with claim C-R2-0023 from round 2; directly applies to our per-layer designer fan-out.

claims.text: Fan-out-then-synthesize is a documented multi-agent pattern: spawn N independent agents to solve the same problem in parallel, then use a synthesis agent to merge the strongest elements; N=3-5 is the efficient range with diminishing returns beyond.
claims.notes: Pattern name and sweet-spot range; directly applies to our Stage 5 fan-out-fan-in.

claims.text: AdaptOrch (arXiv 2602.16873) formalized Diamond topology (fan-out/fan-in) and measured +11.4 percentage point improvement on benchmarks vs single-agent baseline; even misrouted topology choices typically receive second-best performance.
claims.notes: Single benchmark; specific magnitudes academic but pattern validation strong.

claims.text: Best-of-N research shows diminishing returns as N grows — quality gains compress while compute grows linearly; N=3-5 is the efficient range (CarBoN: Calibrated Best-of-N Sampling).
claims.notes: Calibration for fan-out width; we use up to 9 per-layer designers but typical run uses 2-4 based on scope.

claims.text: Parallel agents sharing a filesystem will corrupt each other's work; git checkout changes the working tree for the entire directory and there is no per-process isolation at OS level. Rule: one agent per repository at a time; use separate git worktrees for parallelism.
claims.notes: Production-derived from running 9 AI programs in parallel; informs our per-layer designer output discipline (write only your section).

claims.text: CAID (branch-and-merge based multi-agent system, arXiv 2603.21489) showed dependency-aware task assignment with workspace isolation reduces inter-agent interference; manager prioritizes upstream-end tasks, files with strong/circular dependencies grouped to same engineer.
claims.notes: Single research artifact; pattern direction strong, magnitudes single-sourced.

claims.text: Patterns for resolving parallel-agent contradictions: (a) entity canonicalization (single structured representation before parallel work begins), (b) evidence-based arbitration (each agent surfaces evidence for its conclusion, reconciler assesses evidence strength not vote count), (c) structured contradiction detection (dedicated consistency check before composition), (d) saga-style compensation (compensable steps with explicit rollback).
claims.notes: Four named patterns for cross-layer dependency resolution; informs ADR-0016 design.

claims.text: AI-generated PRDs have documented failure modes: fabricating positive customer reactions, over-precise specs without justification (exact dimensions/weights with no rationale), implementation suggestions leaking into requirements (specifying programming languages or code samples), conflicting statements within document, compliance with irrelevant standards.
claims.notes: Practitioner-observed failure modes; directly informs prd-authoring-knowledge content.

claims.text: AI quality varies by PRD section: HIGH for problem statement, user stories, acceptance criteria, edge cases; MEDIUM for success metrics, open questions; LOW for strategic rationale.
claims.notes: Vendor source (Scriptonia builds PRD tools); calibration is directional rather than authoritative.

claims.text: Practitioner recommendation for AI PRD authoring: use AI as facilitator/sparring partner rather than stenographer; ask AI to propose outline first, then have it ask questions to fill in each section; start new conversation periodically to avoid context rot.
claims.notes: Multi-turn dialogue pattern; matches our synth-intent-clarifier → synth-prd-author handoff.

claims.text: AI generates 8-12 user stories when MVP needs 3-4; recommended correction is to prune rather than accept full list. AI rarely misses story types — it tends toward completeness rather than focus.
claims.notes: Specific magnitude single-sourced; direction of finding (AI over-generates) corroborated by Informal piece.

claims.text: Markdown beats JSON for reasoning tasks: strict JSON-mode constrained decoding routinely shaves 5-15% off reasoning accuracy on math, symbolic, and multi-step analysis tasks; format tax is well-documented but almost universally unmeasured in production.
claims.notes: Critical for our document-heavy pipeline. The 5-15% magnitude single-sourced but theoretical basis (constrained decoding warps probability distribution) is sound.

claims.text: Markdown uses approximately 34-38% fewer tokens than JSON for the same nested content; XML needs about 80% more tokens than markdown.
claims.notes: Specific magnitudes single-sourced; cost direction corroborated by other sources.

claims.text: Format choice principle: use markdown when the model needs to think (reasoning, planning, debugging, weighing context); use strict JSON when output must flow directly into code without human in loop (API responses, tool arguments, database writes). Loose JSON mode (system prompt asking for JSON without strict enforcement) is often worst of both worlds.
claims.notes: Direct guidance for hybrid pipeline; matches our move toward markdown for documents and JSON for metadata.

claims.text: Structured handoff schemas eliminate parse-time ambiguity at agent boundaries; downstream agents reading prose summaries must determine through language understanding where findings end and open questions begin, while schemas make field boundaries explicit. Effect amplifies in longer pipelines: each stage of ambiguity compounds.
claims.notes: Direct evidence that handoff metadata (rationale brief, issues ledger) benefits from structured JSON even when payload is markdown.

claims.text: Constrained decoding (Strict Mode, grammar compilation) provides mathematical guarantees of schema compliance at token level for JSON output; available via OpenAI Strict Mode (August 2024), Anthropic structured output (late 2025), and self-hosted via Outlines/llguidance/XGrammar.
claims.notes: Available for JSON; NOT available for markdown templates — markdown conformance requires application-layer enforcement (i.e., document-reviewer Gate 0).

claims.text: Template-conformance for prose/markdown documents cannot be enforced via constrained decoding (which works at token level for grammars); must be enforced through (a) instruction in knowledge skill teaching the template, (b) post-generation validation via document-reviewer or similar, (c) iterative refinement based on review feedback.
claims.notes: Validates our document-reviewer Gate 0 structural check as the right architecture for markdown template enforcement.

claims.text: Multi-stage review systems work in production: Microsoft Conductor demonstrates parallel specialist reviewers (clarity, readability, accuracy) feeding into synthesis step then human-in-the-loop approval gate. Multi-provider usage (Claude for analysis, separate model for refinement).
claims.notes: Production reference for our multi-stage review architecture (document-reviewer → architecture-auditor → cross-artifact-auditor).

claims.text: Pre-commit review gate pattern (IMTI): adversarial sub-agent reviews working-tree diff before commit, produces verdict CLEAN or findings. Iteration cap: 2 rounds for typical changes, round 3 only if round 2 surfaced substantive bug. Round drift above 2 is a configuration smell, not careful work.
claims.notes: Calibration data point: 2-round cap is sweet spot in production; our 4-cycle cap is conservative but defensible. Watch for theater above 2.

claims.text: STOA Council 3-stage Review System (ADR-061): Stage 1 and 2 evaluate prose artifacts (tickets, plans) through 8-persona LLM jury; Stage 3 evaluates code diffs through 4-axis parallel review. Each stage emits binary Go/Fix/Redo verdict. Global score ≥ 8.0/10 required to Go. Shadow-mode rollout with false-positive < 10% and false-negative < 5% thresholds before mandatory enforcement.
claims.notes: Best-documented production pattern for multi-stage review with calibration thresholds. Verdict shape (Go/Fix/Redo) closely matches document-reviewer's (approved/approved_with_conditions/needs_revision/rejected).

claims.text: Anthropic Building Effective Agents documents voting and orchestrator-workers pattern as core parallelization strategies; tianpan production research recommends explicit spawn guidance: single-agent for fact lookups, 2-3 for moderately complex tasks, 10+ only for tasks requiring genuine parallel investigation.
claims.notes: Calibration data: our up-to-9 per-layer designers is upper end; typical scoped feature should activate 2-4.

claims.text: Codebase analysis output schemas vary across implementations; no industry-standard schema exists. Common patterns include: AST-based extraction (Qodo, codebase-memory-mcp), graph traversal with import/dependency edges (Skopx, GitNexus), evidence-with-provenance fields, multi-modal storage (graph DB + vector DB + history).
claims.notes: Confirms that synth-codebase-researcher output schema (with focusAreas, fact_id, evidence, dataTransformationPipelines) should be pipeline-specified rather than deferring to a standard — there isn't one.

claims.text: Codified Context paper (arXiv 2602.20478) documents three-tier knowledge architecture for AI agents in 108,000-line C# distributed system: hot memory (always-loaded constitution), domain specialists (invoked per task), cold memory (knowledge base retrieved on demand). 19 agent specifications averaging 711 lines (high-capability) and 327 lines (standard-capability). Over half of each specification is project-domain knowledge rather than behavioral instructions.
claims.notes: Validation of our hot/conditional/invocable skill loading pattern. Specific sizes (711/327 lines) align with our 'each agent loads 3-5 skills' rule of thumb.

claims.text: Production pattern from Barnacle.ai (15-agent document writing system, January 2026): sequential execution chosen over parallel due to API rate limits and cost predictability; agents capped at 15 turns; output verification (file existence check) after each agent with up to 3 retries; post-processing deduplication agent runs after all sections written.
claims.notes: Production tradeoffs: parallelism is not always the answer. Rate limits, cost predictability, and verification overhead matter. Informs our 'conditional preload top 5' rather than 'all 9 designers always run'.
